content.title: Verb Forms and Non-Finite Structures
content.overview: This lesson focuses on distinguishing between main verbs and non-finite verb forms—infinitives, gerunds, and participles. Mastering these structures ensures that every verb phrase in a sentence correctly matches its grammatical function and logical purpose.
learning_objectives: Distinguish between main verbs and non-finite verb forms (infinitives, gerunds, and participles).
Identify the correct verb form required by specific auxiliary verbs or sentence slots.
Apply the 'Form-and-Function Check' to ensure grammatical attachment and logical time sequence.

sections.title: Understanding Non-Finite Verb Forms
sections.content: Non-finite verbs are verb forms that do not function as the main predicate of a clause. They include: 1. Infinitives (to + base form, e.g., 'to run'), which often express purpose or follow specific verbs like 'hope' or 'want'. 2. Gerunds (-ing form, e.g., 'running'), which function as nouns. 3. Participles (present -ing or past -ed/-en), which function as adjectives or parts of multi-word verb phrases. Unlike main verbs, non-finite forms do not change based on the subject's number or person.

sections.title: Main Verbs and Auxiliaries
sections.content: Main verbs often require auxiliary (helping) verbs to indicate tense or mood. A common ACT trap involves using the wrong form after an auxiliary. Use the base form after modal auxiliaries (e.g., 'must go', 'will see'). Use the past participle after 'have' to form perfect tenses (e.g., 'has driven', 'had eaten'). Use the present participle after 'be' for continuous tenses (e.g., 'is walking').

sections.title: The Form-and-Function Check
sections.content: To solve verb form questions, first identify the 'slot' the word occupies. If the word follows a preposition or acts as a subject, it is likely a gerund. If it follows a verb of intent or purpose, it is likely an infinitive. If it modifies a noun, it is a participle. Once the slot is identified, replace the underlined portion with the simplest version of that form to see if it sounds correct, then check for proper time sequencing (e.g., using 'to have finished' for an action completed before another point in time).

worked_examples.question: Identify the best revision: The scientist, [having discovering] a new element, published her findings immediately.
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the slot: The phrase modifies 'The scientist,' so it is a participial phrase. 2. Evaluate the form: 'Having discovering' is ungrammatical because 'having' requires a past participle. 3. Correct the form: Change 'discovering' to 'discovered.' The correct phrase is 'having discovered,' which indicates the action was completed before the publishing. 4. Final check: 'The scientist, having discovered a new element, published...' is grammatically sound.

worked_examples.question: Choose the correct form: The team was eager [to having started] the project, but the budget was delayed.
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the slot: The phrase follows the adjective 'eager,' which typically takes an infinitive. 2. Evaluate the form: 'To having started' is a redundant mix of an infinitive and a gerund. 3. Simplify: The standard infinitive is 'to start.' 4. Check meaning: 'Eager to start' correctly expresses the team's desire. The correct sentence is 'The team was eager to start the project...'

common_mistakes: Using a gerund (-ing) when an infinitive (to + verb) is required by the preceding verb (e.g., saying 'decided going' instead of 'decided to go').
Confusing the past tense (simple past) with the past participle (e.g., using 'have went' instead of 'have gone').
Misplacing a participial modifier so it appears to describe the wrong noun.
Using 'to + -ing' (e.g., 'to walking') when a simple infinitive or a simple gerund is needed.
exam_tips: If you see 'to' followed by an '-ing' word, be suspicious; it is rarely correct unless 'to' is acting as a preposition (e.g., 'committed to winning').
When a verb follows 'have,' 'has,' or 'had,' it must be in the past participle form.
Check for parallelism: if a list contains two gerunds, the third item should also be a gerund.
content.recap: Verb forms must match their grammatical role. Use the Form-and-Function Check to determine if a word is a main verb, gerund, infinitive, or participle. Ensure auxiliaries are followed by the correct participle or base form, and maintain parallelism in lists of non-finite verbs.

knowledge_claims.content: An infinitive is a non-finite verb form consisting of the word 'to' plus the base form of the verb.
A gerund is a verb form ending in '-ing' that functions as a noun within a sentence.
Modal auxiliaries such as 'must,' 'will,' 'can,' and 'should' must be followed by the base form of the verb without 'to'.
The auxiliary verbs 'have,' 'has,' and 'had' must be followed by the past participle form of the verb to create perfect tenses.
To verify a verb form, identify its grammatical slot: main verb, noun (gerund), adjective (participle), or purpose/intent (infinitive).
A perfect infinitive (to + have + past participle) is used to indicate an action that was intended or expected to be completed before a specific time.
It is a grammatical error to use a present participle (-ing) immediately after the word 'to' when 'to' is part of an infinitive structure.
Participial phrases function as adjectives and must be placed near the noun they modify to avoid confusion.
Unlike main verbs, non-finite verb forms (infinitives, gerunds, and participles) do not change their form to agree with the subject's number or person.
When checking for parallelism, ensure that all non-finite verbs in a series share the same form, such as all gerunds or all infinitives.
The auxiliary verb 'be' (am, is, are, was, were) is followed by the present participle (-ing) to form continuous tenses.
Use a gerund when the verb form follows a preposition, such as in the phrase 'interested in learning.'

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 5: Seeds Across the Block
[1] During the first warm weekend in March [[volunteers at a community garden was]] preparing to organize a seed exchange for neighborhood growers. The group defined a successful result in advance and noted which conditions would be held constant during each comparison. [2] several envelopes arrived with only a plant name. [[Nevertheless,]] volunteers added a brief labeling station at the entrance. [3] The writer is considering deleting the following sentence: “the most useful notes described shade, soil, and harvest time.” Once the revision was in place, the group repeated the same measurements rather than relying on appearance alone. The final record included both the unsuccessful condition and the revised one, making the basis for the decision visible to someone who had not watched the work. [4] The final design was [[a design that was successful]]: gardeners could compare varieties before choosing seeds. [5] Which conclusion best emphasizes that the exchange turned individual experience into a shared local record?

Which replacement for the wording marked [1] is grammatically acceptable and most concise while preserving the completed time frame?

options.F: volunteers at a community garden was preparing
options.G: preparing was volunteers at a community garden
options.H: volunteers at a community garden, prepared
options.J: volunteers at a community garden prepared

items.explanation: The simple past tense concisely expresses the completed action and agrees with the subject.

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 5: Shade at the Bus Stop
[1] During the hottest week of June [[a youth planning council was]] preparing to compare shade designs for four exposed bus stops. The group defined a successful result in advance and noted which conditions would be held constant during each comparison. [2] one proposed canopy blocked a storefront sign. [[Nevertheless,]] the council rotated and shortened the canopy. [3] The writer is considering deleting the following sentence: “a narrow roof cooled the bench at noon but missed it by late afternoon.” Once the revision was in place, the group repeated the same measurements rather than relying on appearance alone. The final record included both the unsuccessful condition and the revised one, making the basis for the decision visible to someone who had not watched the work. [4] The final design was [[a design that was successful]]: the revised design shaded the bench without hiding the sign. [5] Which conclusion best emphasizes that the recommendation joined measured heat data with the needs of nearby businesses?

Which replacement for the wording marked [1] is grammatically acceptable and most concise while preserving the completed time frame?

options.F: a youth planning council was preparing
options.G: preparing was a youth planning council

items.explanation: The simple past tense concisely expresses the completed action and agrees with the subject.

videoLesson.title: Verify Verb Forms and Nonfinite Structures
videoLesson.description: Recognize whether a phrase functions as a main verb, auxiliary verb phrase, gerund, infinitive, or participial modifier. Replace mentally with the simplest correct form and check attachment, agreement, and parallelism.
